tool.name: AccuracySampleSize

summary.para: Estimates the reference sample size needed for a statistically defensible accuracy assessment. Pick one of four methods: Congalton and Green's multinomial approach (Tortora 1978) as the worst case with no map proportions known, refined by the largest class proportion, or from per-class proportions with individual precision requirements -- each with the optional finite population correction -- or the Olofsson et al. (2014) sample size for a target standard error of overall accuracy. Returns the recommended size as a derived output for ModelBuilder. A port of the classic extension's Sample Size tool. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
Answers "how many reference samples do I need?" before the field work -- the question that determines whether an accuracy assessment will be statistically defensible. The Estimation method drop-down picks one of four estimators, and only that method's parameters stay enabled. The multinomial methods follow Congalton and Green's approach (after Tortora 1978), exactly as in the classic Kappa extension, whose published example table this port reproduces to the sample.
The four methods, by how much you know: • Worst case (no class proportions known). Only the number of classes, the confidence level, and the desired precision. The worst case (a class at exactly 50%) is assumed; this gives the largest safe answer. • Largest class proportion known. Also enter the largest class's map proportion -- since proportions sum to 100%, the largest class is always the one closest to 50%, and its variance governs the sample size. The farther it sits from 50%, the more the estimate tightens below the worst case. • Per-class proportions and precisions. Fill the precisions table with each class's proportion and its own required precision -- the acceptable confidence-interval half-width for that class's accuracy estimate, a statement about the quality of the estimate you want. The most demanding class governs, and the class count comes from the table; tightening precision on one critical class raises the total accordingly. • Target standard error of overall accuracy (Olofsson et al. 2014). The planning route for modern area-weighted assessments (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015): choose a target standard error for overall accuracy (in percentage points) and fill the user's-accuracies table with proportions and conjectured user's accuracies -- your best guess of how accurate the map actually is per class, a statement about the map rather than the estimate. If you expect 19 out of 20 mapped cells of a class to be correct [i.e. 95%], enter 95; if you expect only half of them to be correct, enter 50. Equation 13 gives the total n; guesses nearer 50% demand more samples, so an honest or slightly pessimistic guess is the conservative choice. Olofsson et al. also recommend allocating 50-100 samples to rare-but-important classes and distributing the rest proportionally.
The finite population correction (the three multinomial methods; Thompson 2002, Sampling, 2nd ed.) applies when only a limited number of samples is possible (e.g., a photo-interpretation frame of N plots): the required n shrinks as n approaches N.
Rules of thumb (Congalton and Green): a minimum of ~50 samples per class, 75-100 with many classes (over 12), and never leave a class unsampled -- accuracy cannot be estimated for a class that was never checked.
Outputs. The report in the messages and optionally as a text file -- closing with a ready-to-run R cross-check of the chosen method, your numbers baked in, to copy and paste straight into R -- and, for ModelBuilder chains, the recommended sample size as a derived output (with the finite population correction applied when a population is given), ready to feed the number-of-points parameter of the Random Point Generator or the sample size of Select Random Records.
Once you have the number, draw the design with the Random Point Generator (stratified by map class, with spacing options) or select from an existing frame with Select Random Records; then run the assessment with the Classification Accuracy (Kappa) tool.

dialogReference.para: Which of the four estimators to run; only that method's parameters stay enabled. Worst case: nothing known beyond the class count -- the largest safe answer. Largest class proportion known: tightens the worst case using the largest class's proportion (always the one closest to 50%). Per-class proportions and precisions: the most demanding class governs. Target standard error (Olofsson et al. 2014): the planning route for area-weighted assessments, from conjectured user's accuracies.
How many classes the map distinguishes. The confidence level is Bonferroni-shared across them, so more classes require more samples. For the per-class methods the count comes from the table instead.
The probability the sample will support statistically valid accuracy conclusions (default 95).
The acceptable half-width of the accuracy estimates (default 10). Tighter precision raises the sample size quadratically.

The map proportion of the largest class. Because proportions sum to 100%, the largest class is always the one closest to 50% -- the class with the greatest variance, which governs the sample size. (With exactly two classes the two proportions are equally distant from 50%, so either works.) Read it from the classified raster's attribute table or the polygon areas.

param.name: class_table
param.displayname: Per-class proportions and required precisions (one row per class)

dialogReference.para: One row per class: its map proportion (percent) and its required precision (percent) -- how tightly you need that class's accuracy estimate pinned down, the acceptable half-width of its confidence interval. It is a statement about the quality of the estimate you want, not about how accurate you expect the map to be. Tighter precision on any class raises the total sample size, and the most demanding class governs.

param.name: ua_table
param.displayname: Per-class proportions and conjectured user's accuracies (one row per class)

dialogReference.para: One row per class: its map proportion (percent) and its conjectured user's accuracy (percent, 0 - 100) -- your best planning guess of how accurate the map actually is for that class. If you expect 19 out of 20 mapped cells of the class to be correct [i.e. 95%], enter 95; if you expect only half of them to be correct, enter 50. It is a statement about the map, not about the estimate you want (that is the other table's "required precision"): Olofsson et al. (2014) use each guess for its stratum's standard deviation. Guesses nearer 50% are conservative -- an inaccurate map needs many more samples to pin its overall accuracy to the same target -- so guess low when unsure.
Optional: the total number of possible samples (a fixed plot frame). The finite population correction shrinks the required n, and the derived recommended size carries it.

param.name: target_se
param.displayname: Target standard error of overall accuracy (percent, 0 - 100; e.g. 1)

dialogReference.para: The target standard error for overall accuracy, in percentage points -- e.g. 1 means the overall-accuracy estimate should carry a standard error of about one percentage point (the Classification Accuracy report prints its achieved standard errors as proportions; 1% = 0.01). Used with the per-class table's proportions and conjectured user's accuracies (Olofsson et al. 2014, eq. 13).
A text file holding the sample-size report (it also prints in the messages). The .txt extension is added automatically if omitted.

The recommended sample size for the chosen method, with the finite population correction applied when a population was given -- connect it to the Random Point Generator or Select Random Records in ModelBuilder.

scriptExample.title: Estimate Sample Size example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The classic manual's scenario: four classes at 95% confidence and 10% precision with the largest class at 36.7%, over a 10,000-plot frame.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path result = arcpy.jenness.AccuracySampleSize( method="Largest class proportion known", n_classes=4, confidence=95, precision=10, max_prop=36.7, population=10000) print(result.getOutput(1)) # the recommended sample size
